claim: The Rasgrp1Anaef mutation is an ENU-induced missense variant with an A to G nucleotide change in codon 519 within exon 13 of the Rasgrp1 gene.
source: Sequencing of the exons of Rasgrp1, the only gene within this interval with a known immune function, identified an A to G missense mutation in codon 519 within exon 13 (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the identification of the specific mutation through sequencing.

claim: The Rasgrp1Anaef mutation results in substitution of arginine with glycine at position 519 (R519G) in the second EF hand of Rasgrp1.
source: The mutant codon, located in Rasgrp1's second EF hand (EF2), encodes a neutral amino acid glycine (G) instead of the normal arginine (R), a large polar molecule with a positive charge (Rasgrp1 R519G; Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the amino acid substitution and its location in the protein structure.

claim: The R519G substitution causes an approximate 40% decrease in Rasgrp1 protein levels in homozygous Rasgrp1Anaef/Anaef thymocytes.
source: The R519G substitution caused an approximate 40% decrease in Rasgrp1 protein levels in homozygous Rasgrp1Anaef/Anaef thymocytes (Figure 2F).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 2F demonstrates reduced protein expression levels.

claim: Heterozygous Rasgrp1Anaef/+ mice exhibit abnormal immune phenotypes despite expressing more Rasgrp1 protein than heterozygous Rasgrp1+/− mice.
source: Since heterozygous Rasgrp1+/− thymocytes express half the Rasgrp1 dosage (Figure 2G) but do not display an abnormal immune phenotype (Dower et al., 2000), whereas heterozygous Rasgrp1Anaef/+ mice do exhibit abnormal immune phenotypes (Figure 1B,D), we conclude that the immune dysregulation in mice bearing the Rasgrp1Anaef allele is caused by the specific R519G alteration and not simply by a reduction of Rasgrp1 protein levels.
evidence: The manuscript compares phenotypes between different genotypes and cites previous work on Rasgrp1+/− mice.

claim: Rasgrp1Anaef mice have normal frequencies and numbers of mature CD4+ and CD8+ single positive thymocyte subsets.
source: The frequency and number of mature CD4+ and CD8+ single positive (SP) thymocyte subsets was normal in Rasgrp1Anaef mice, whereas these subsets were markedly decreased in Rasgrp1−/− (knockout) mice analyzed in parallel (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 3A,B shows comparable thymocyte subset frequencies and numbers between wildtype and Rasgrp1Anaef mice.

claim: The Rasgrp1Anaef mutation does not decrease the frequency of CD69hi TCRβhi cells amongst CD4+CD8+ double positive thymocytes.
source: Unlike the knockout allele, the Rasgrp1Anaef mutation did not decrease the frequency of CD69hi TCRβhi cells amongst CD4+CD8+ double positive (DP) thymocytes (Figure 3C)
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis in Figure 3C demonstrates normal frequencies of CD69hi TCRβhi DP cells.

claim: The Rasgrp1Anaef mutation does not affect the number of Foxp3+ CD4SP cells in the thymus.
source: Unlike the knockout allele, the Rasgrp1Anaef mutation did not decrease...the number of Foxp3+ CD4SP cells in the thymus (Figure 3B).
evidence: Quantification in Figure 3B shows normal numbers of Foxp3+ CD4SP thymocytes.

claim: Rasgrp1Anaef thymocytes exhibit no competitive disadvantage as they mature from DP to SP cells in bone marrow chimeras.
source: Even in bone marrow chimeras reconstituted with a mixture of CD45.2+ Rasgrp1Anaef and CD45.1+ wildtype marrow, the Rasgrp1Anaef thymocytes exhibited no competitive disadvantage as they matured from DP to SP cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: Competitive reconstitution experiments in Figure 3D show equal representation of Rasgrp1Anaef cells across thymocyte subsets.

claim: The kinetics of maturation from DP to SP thymocytes is unaffected by the Rasgrp1Anaef mutation as measured by BrdU pulse-labeling.
source: Injection into mice of 5-bromo-2′-deoxyuridine (BrdU) to pulse-label a cohort of proliferating DP thymocytes followed by analysis on day 5 demonstrated that the kinetics of maturation into SP cells was unaffected by the Rasgrp1Anaef mutation (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: BrdU labeling experiments in Figure 3E show similar maturation kinetics between wildtype and Rasgrp1Anaef thymocytes.

claim: Rasgrp1Anaef mice show normal deletion of Vβ5+ and Vβ11+ SP thymocytes upon self-superantigen/I-Ek recognition in B10.Br mice.
source: There was also normal deletion of Vβ5+ and Vβ11+ SP thymocytes upon self-superantigen/I-Ek recognition in B10.Br mice (Figure 3F)
evidence: Analysis in Figure 3F demonstrates comparable negative selection of superantigen-reactive T cells.

claim: Rasgrp1Anaef and wildtype CD4SP thymocytes show similar usage of TCRα Jα segments.
source: There was also...similar usage of TCRα Jα segments in wildtype and Rasgrp1Anaef CD4SP thymocyte populations (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: PCR analysis of Jα segment usage in Figure 3G shows comparable patterns between genotypes.

claim: The Rasgrp1Anaef mutation results in impaired membrane recruitment of Rasgrp1 in response to PMA stimulation.
source: PMA stimulation resulted in membrane recruitment and cytoplasmic clearing of wildtype Rasgrp1; whereas these events were decreased for Rasgrp1Anaef (Figure 4F).
evidence: Microscopy data in Figure 4F shows reduced membrane localization of Rasgrp1Anaef compared to wildtype.

claim: Rasgrp1Anaef is hypomorphic for activating the Ras-ERK pathway in JPRM441 cells stimulated with PMA and ionomycin.
source: Gating on cells with different GFP intensities (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) revealed that Rasgrp1Anaef was hypomorphic (partial loss of function) for activating the Ras-ERK pathway: in GFP+ cells expressing Rasgrp1Anaef there was only low ERK phosphorylation (P-ERK) and this was only modestly increased when PMA and ionomycin were added (Figure 4A).
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis in Figure 4A demonstrates reduced ERK phosphorylation in cells expressing Rasgrp1Anaef.

claim: Rasgrp1Anaef decreases PMA-induced GTP-loading of Ras to levels below that of nontransfected JPRM441 cells.
source: Since JPRM441 cells do not express surface TCR (Roose et al., 2005), clonal cell lines were stimulated with PMA followed by RasGTP pull-down assays, which demonstrated that Rasgrp1Anaef decreased PMA-induced GTP-loading of Ras to levels below that of the nontransfected JPRM441 cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: RasGTP pull-down assays in Figure 4B show reduced Ras activation in Rasgrp1Anaef-expressing cells.

claim: Rasgrp1Anaef exhibits a dominant negative effect on Ras-ERK signaling in JPRM441 cells.
source: In fact, P-ERK responses in JPRM441-Rasgrp1Anaef cells were more impaired than in the parental JPRM441 cells, indicating a dominant negative effect, which was also observed at the level of Ras activation (Figure 4B).
evidence: Comparison of P-ERK responses shows that Rasgrp1Anaef expression reduces signaling below baseline JPRM441 levels.

claim: Rasgrp1Anaef thymocytes show drastically impaired phosphorylation of T184-Rasgrp1 and reduced ERK phosphorylation in response to anti-CD3 stimulation.
source: Using a new monoclonal antibody specific for P-T184-Rasgrp1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) we observed drastically impaired phosphorylation of T184-Rasgrp1, and reduced ERK phosphorylation in Rasgrp1Anaef thymocytes (Figure 5A).
evidence: Western blot analysis in Figure 5A demonstrates reduced phosphorylation of both T184-Rasgrp1 and ERK.

claim: Rasgrp1+/− thymocytes heterozygous for the null allele display readily detectable Rasgrp1- and ERK-phosphorylation.
source: By contrast, Rasgrp1+/− thymocytes heterozygous for the null allele displayed readily detectable Rasgrp1- and ERK- phosphorylation (Figure 5B)
evidence: Western blot in Figure 5B shows normal phosphorylation patterns in Rasgrp1+/− cells.

claim: The signaling defects in Rasgrp1Anaef thymocytes are much greater than when the amount of Rasgrp1 is simply halved.
source: By contrast, Rasgrp1+/− thymocytes heterozygous for the null allele displayed readily detectable Rasgrp1- and ERK- phosphorylation (Figure 5B), demonstrating that the signaling defects in the Rasgrp1Anaef thymocytes are much greater than when the amount of Rasgrp1 is simply halved.
evidence: Comparison between Rasgrp1Anaef and Rasgrp1+/− phenotypes demonstrates a qualitative difference beyond protein dosage.

claim: Rasgrp1Anaef thymocytes show reduced anti-CD3- and PMA-induced P-ERK responses in DP, CD4SP, and CD8SP subsets.
source: Thymocyte subset-specific P-ERK analyses revealed reduced anti-CD3- and PMA-induced responses in DP, CD4SP, and CD8SP Rasgrp1Anaef thymocytes (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis in Figure 5C shows reduced ERK phosphorylation across multiple thymocyte subsets.

claim: Rasgrp1Anaef TCR-transgenic thymocytes show a small decrease in positive selection compared to wildtype controls when TCR transgenes are prematurely expressed at high levels on DP thymocytes.
source: When pressure was placed on TCR-Ras-ERK signaling for positive selection in vivo, by introducing any one of three different rearranged TCR transgenes that are prematurely expressed at higher than normal levels on DP thymocytes, a small decrease in positive selection was revealed in Rasgrp1Anaef TCR-transgenic thymocytes compared to their wildtype controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Analysis of three different TCR transgenic models in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 shows modest reductions in positive selection.

claim: The low affinity pMHC stimulation that drives physiological positive selection in vivo is remarkably robust to decreased Rasgrp1 activation of Ras-ERK.
source: Collectively, these results lead to the surprising conclusion that the low affinity pMHC stimulation that drives physiological positive selection in vivo is remarkably robust to decreased Rasgrp1 activation of Ras-ERK.
evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the observation of normal positive selection despite reduced Ras-ERK signaling in vitro.

claim: Rasgrp1Anaef mice exhibit elevated frequencies of CD44hi CD4+ cells in peripheral blood.
source: As part of a mouse genome-wide screen for immune phenotypes induced by ENU mutagenesis (Nelms and Goodnow, 2001), we identified a variant C57BL/6 (B6) pedigree displaying elevated frequencies of CD44hi CD4+ cells (Figure 1A)
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 1A shows increased CD44hi CD4+ cell frequencies.

claim: Rasgrp1Anaef mice show elevated CD44 expression on naïve FOXP3− CD44lo CD4+ cells.
source: As part of a mouse genome-wide screen for immune phenotypes induced by ENU mutagenesis (Nelms and Goodnow, 2001), we identified a variant C57BL/6 (B6) pedigree displaying...elevated CD44 expression on naïve FOXP3− CD44lo CD4+ cells (Figure 1B)
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis in Figure 1B demonstrates increased CD44 MFI on naïve CD4+ cells.

claim: Rasgrp1Anaef mice produce antinuclear antibodies with a homogeneous nuclear staining pattern.
source: As part of a mouse genome-wide screen for immune phenotypes induced by ENU mutagenesis (Nelms and Goodnow, 2001), we identified a variant C57BL/6 (B6) pedigree displaying...antinuclear antibodies (ANAs) staining with a homogeneous nuclear pattern (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Immunofluorescence on HEp-2 cells in Figure 1C,D shows homogeneous nuclear ANA staining.

claim: ANAs are present in 70% of homozygous Rasgrp1Anaef/Anaef mice and 35% of heterozygous Rasgrp1Anaef/+ mice, compared to 5% of wildtype B6 mice.
source: ANAs were present in 70% of homozygous Rasgrp1Anaef/Anaef mice and 35% of heterozygous Rasgrp1Anaef/+ mice (Figure 1D), compared to 5% of wildtype B6 mice, indicating a gene dosage effect.
evidence: Quantification in Figure 1D shows the frequency of ANA-positive mice by genotype.

claim: The frequency of activated or memory CD44hi Foxp3− CD4+ cells increases in Rasgrp1Anaef mice between 50 and 150 days of age.
source: Total splenocyte numbers and CD4 subsets were within the normal range in young Rasgrp1Anaef animals, but between 50 and 150 days of age the frequencies of activated or memory CD44hi Foxp3− CD4+ cells increased, as did Foxp3+ CD4 cells, while the frequency of CD44low Foxp3− naïve CD4+ cells decreased (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis over time in Figure 6A-C shows age-dependent changes in CD4+ subset frequencies.

claim: The frequency of Foxp3+ CD4 cells increases in Rasgrp1Anaef mice between 50 and 150 days of age.
source: Total splenocyte numbers and CD4 subsets were within the normal range in young Rasgrp1Anaef animals, but between 50 and 150 days of age the frequencies of activated or memory CD44hi Foxp3− CD4+ cells increased, as did Foxp3+ CD4 cells, while the frequency of CD44low Foxp3− naïve CD4+ cells decreased (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 6A-C shows increased Foxp3+ CD4+ cell frequencies with age.

claim: The frequency of CD44low Foxp3− naïve CD4+ cells decreases in Rasgrp1Anaef mice between 50 and 150 days of age.
source: Total splenocyte numbers and CD4 subsets were within the normal range in young Rasgrp1Anaef animals, but between 50 and 150 days of age the frequencies of activated or memory CD44hi Foxp3− CD4+ cells increased, as did Foxp3+ CD4 cells, while the frequency of CD44low Foxp3− naïve CD4+ cells decreased (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis in Figure 6A-C demonstrates decreased naïve CD4+ cell frequencies with age.

claim: Interferon-γ producing cells are increased in frequency in Rasgrp1Anaef mice by a similar magnitude as CD44hi cells as a whole.
source: Further resolution of CD4+ subsets based on intracellular cytokine staining revealed that interferon-γ producing cells were increased in frequency by a similar magnitude as CD44hi cells as a whole (Figure 6D and data not shown).
evidence: Intracellular cytokine staining in Figure 6D shows increased IFNγ+ cells proportional to overall CD44hi expansion.

claim: The Rasgrp1Anaef mutation does not skew T-helper cells towards a Th1 phenotype, but simply increases the number of activated or memory/effector CD4+ cells.
source: Thus, there was no evidence that the Rasgrp1Anaef mutation skewed T-helper cells towards a Th1 phenotype, but simply increased the number of activated or memory/effector CD4+ cells.
evidence: The conclusion is based on proportional increases in IFNγ+ cells relative to total CD44hi cells without preferential Th1 skewing.

claim: Rasgrp1Anaef mice show a dramatic expansion of T follicular helper (TFH) cells identified by high expression of PD-1 and CXCR5 on CD4+ cells.
source: Staining for PD-1 and CXCR5, whose high expression on CD4+ cells identifies T follicular helper (TFH) cells (Ramiscal and Vinuesa, 2013) revealed a dramatic expansion of these cells in Rasgrp1Anaef mice (Figure 6E).
evidence: Flow cytometry in Figure 6E shows increased frequency of CXCR5+ PD-1hi TFH cells.

claim: Most of the increase in CD44hi Foxp3− CD4+ cells in Rasgrp1Anaef mice is due to a 600% increase in cells expressing intermediate levels of PD-1 and CXCR5 that are distinguished by high expression of Helios.
source: However most of the increase in CD44hi Foxp3− CD4+ cells in Rasgrp1Anaef mice was due to a 600% increase in cells that expressed intermediate levels of PD-1 and CXCR5, and hence are unlikely to be TFH cells, but were distinguished by high expression of the Helios transcription factor (Figure 6E).
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis in Figure 6E quantifies the expansion of Helios+ PD-1+ CXCR5int cells.

claim: Helios is highly expressed in Foxp3+ T-reg cells.
source: Helios is highly expressed in Foxp3+ T-reg cells (Thornton et al., 2010)
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on Helios expression in T-reg cells.

claim: In wildtype and Rasgrp1Anaef mice, Helios is upregulated in a subset of Foxp3− CD4+ cells, nearly all of which are CD44hi.
source: Helios is highly expressed in Foxp3+ T-reg cells (Thornton et al., 2010), but in wildtype and Rasgrp1Anaef mice Helios is also upregulated in a subset of Foxp3− CD4+ cells, nearly all of which are CD44hi (Figure 6F).
evidence: Flow cytometry in Figure 6F shows Helios expression predominantly in CD44hi Foxp3− CD4+ cells.

claim: Rasgrp1Anaef greatly increases the Helios+ CD44hi Foxp3− CD4+ population, which is distinguished by high PD-1 expression.
source: Rasgrp1Anaef greatly increased this Helios+ CD44hi Foxp3− CD4+ population, which was also distinguished by high PD-1 expression in Rasgrp1Anaef (Figure 6F).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 6F demonstrates expansion and PD-1 expression on Helios+ CD44hi Foxp3− cells.

claim: Rasgrp1Anaef mice have normal frequencies of CD95 (Fas)+ GL-7+ germinal center B cells in the spleen.
source: Rasgrp1Anaef mice had normal frequencies of CD95 (Fas)+ GL-7+ germinal center B cells in the spleen (Figure 6G)
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis in Figure 6G shows comparable germinal center B cell frequencies.

claim: The accumulating Helios+ PD-1+ CXCR5int Foxp3− CD44hi CD4+ cells in Rasgrp1Anaef mice are a distinct type of activated CD4+ cell but not fully differentiated TFH cells.
source: Rasgrp1Anaef mice had normal frequencies of CD95 (Fas)+ GL-7+ germinal center B cells in the spleen (Figure 6G), consistent with the conclusion that the accumulating Helios+ PD-1+ CXCR5int Foxp3− CD44hi CD4+ cells were a distinct type of activated CD4+ cell but not fully differentiated TFH cells.
evidence: The conclusion is based on normal germinal center B cell frequencies and intermediate CXCR5 expression.

claim: Accumulation of PD-1+ Helios+ CD4+ T cells in Rasgrp1Anaef mice is profoundly suppressed in the absence of B cells.
source: In Rasgrp1Anaef Cd79anull animals lacking B cells, accumulation of PD-1+ Helios+ CD4+ T cells was profoundly suppressed (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis in Figure 7A,B shows reduced PD-1+ Helios+ CD4+ cells in B cell-deficient mice.

claim: The Rasgrp1Anaef-driven distortion in relative frequencies of naïve, effector/memory and regulatory subsets of CD4 splenocytes is rectified by the absence of B cells.
source: Indeed, the Rasgrp1Anaef–driven distortion in relative frequencies of naïve, effector/memory and regulatory subsets of CD4 splenocytes was rectified by the absence of B cells in Rasgrp1Anaef Cd79anull mice (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 7C,D demonstrates normalization of CD4+ subset frequencies in B cell-deficient Rasgrp1Anaef mice.

claim: The elevated CD44 expression on naïve CD4+ cells in Rasgrp1Anaef mice is still present in the absence of B cells.
source: By contrast, the elevated CD44 expression on naïve CD4+ cells was still present (Figure 7E) indicating this is a constitutive effect of the Rasgrp1Anaef mutation.
evidence: Flow cytometry in Figure 7E shows maintained elevated CD44 expression on naïve cells in B cell-deficient mice.

claim: The elevated CD44 expression on naïve CD4+ cells is a constitutive effect of the Rasgrp1Anaef mutation.
source: By contrast, the elevated CD44 expression on naïve CD4+ cells was still present (Figure 7E) indicating this is a constitutive effect of the Rasgrp1Anaef mutation.
evidence: The persistence of elevated CD44 in the absence of B cells indicates it is a cell-intrinsic effect.

claim: A high proportion of chimeric mice with Rasgrp1Anaef in T cells but not B cells develop antinuclear autoantibodies comparable to mice where both B and T cells carry the Anaef mutation.
source: Despite having the Anaef mutation in the T but not B cells of group B mice, a high proportion developed antinuclear autoantibodies comparable to the control group D where both B and T cells carried the Anaef mutation (Figure 7G).
evidence: ANA testing in chimeric mice in Figure 7G shows comparable autoantibody frequencies regardless of B cell genotype.

claim: A high frequency and number of CD45.2+ Rasgrp1Anaef CD4+ T cells acquire a Helios+ PD-1+ phenotype in chimeric mice where the Anaef mutation is excluded from B cells.
source: Moreover, a high frequency and number of CD45.2+ Rasgrp1Anaef CD4+ T cells acquired a Helios+ PD-1+ phenotype in Group B animals, unlike the co-resident CD45.1+ wildtype T cells (Figure 7I).
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis in Figure 7I shows cell-autonomous accumulation of Helios+ PD-1+ phenotype in Rasgrp1Anaef T cells.

claim: The accumulation of activated CD4 T cells in Rasgrp1Anaef mice reflects a cell-autonomous effect of the Anaef mutation within the CD4 T cells and does not depend upon the Anaef allele being present in B cells.
source: The accumulation of these activated CD4 T cells thus reflects a cell-autonomous effect of the Anaef mutation within the CD4 T cells and does not depend upon the Anaef allele being present in B cells.
evidence: The conclusion is drawn from chimera experiments showing T cell-intrinsic effects independent of B cell genotype.

claim: The chino mouse strain has decreased CD44 expression on peripheral CD4+ CD62Lhi cells but relatively normal T cell numbers and subsets.
source: In our ongoing peripheral blood screen of ENU mutagenized mouse pedigrees, we identified a strain, chino, with decreased CD44 expression on peripheral CD4+ CD62Lhi cells but relatively normal T cell numbers and subsets (Figure 8A).
evidence: Flow cytometry screening identified the chino phenotype as shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The chino phenotype maps to a single nucleotide change (T to G) in exon 5 of the Mtor gene, introducing serine in place of isoleucine at position 205 (I205S) in the fifth predicted HEAT domain.
source: This unusual phenotype mapped to a single nucleotide change (T to G) in exon 5 of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (Mtor) gene, introducing serine in place of isoleucine at position 205 in the fifth predicted HEAT domain of the protein (Knutson, 2010) (Figure 8B).
evidence: Genetic mapping and sequencing identified the specific mutation in Mtor as shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The mTOR isoleucine residue at position 205 is entirely conserved from mammals to yeast.
source: This mTOR isoleucine residue is entirely conserved from mammals to yeast (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Sequence alignment in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 demonstrates evolutionary conservation of the residue.

claim: Mtorchino/chino mice are viable but slightly smaller than wildtype.
source: As the absence of Mtor is embryonic lethal in mice (Gangloff et al., 2004; Murakami et al., 2004), the fact that Mtorchino/chino (hereafter referred to as Mtorchino) mice are viable but slightly smaller than wildtype (Figure 8C) indicates that the Mtorchino allele retains substantial function.
evidence: Body mass measurements in Figure 8C show reduced size in Mtorchino mice compared to wildtype.

claim: The Mtorchino allele retains substantial mTOR function.
source: As the absence of Mtor is embryonic lethal in mice (Gangloff et al., 2004; Murakami et al., 2004), the fact that Mtorchino/chino (hereafter referred to as Mtorchino) mice are viable but slightly smaller than wildtype (Figure 8C) indicates that the Mtorchino allele retains substantial function.
evidence: Viability of Mtorchino mice contrasts with embryonic lethality of Mtor null mice, indicating partial function.

claim: TCR-induced phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6 (P-S6) is modestly decreased but not abolished in Mtorchino CD4+ splenocytes.
source: Consistent with a subtle decrease in mTOR activity, TCR-induced phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6 (P-S6) was modestly decreased but not abolished in Mtorchino CD4+ splenocytes (Figure 8D).
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis in Figure 8D shows reduced but detectable P-S6 induction in Mtorchino cells.

claim: The numbers of DP, CD4SP and CD8SP thymocytes are normal in Mtorchino mice.
source: The numbers of DP, CD4SP and CD8SP thymocytes were normal in Mtorchino mice (Figure 8E).
evidence: Quantification in Figure 8E shows comparable thymocyte subset numbers between wildtype and Mtorchino mice.

claim: Expression of CD69, CD5 and TCRβ on DP and SP thymocytes is normal in Mtorchino mice.
source: Whereas expression of CD69, CD5 and TCRβ on DP and SP thymocytes was normal, CD44 expression was decreased on Mtorchino CD4SP and CD8SP thymocytes (Figure 8F).
evidence: Flow cytometry histograms in Figure 8F show normal expression of CD69, CD5, and TCRβ.

claim: CD44 expression is decreased on Mtorchino CD4SP and CD8SP thymocytes.
source: Whereas expression of CD69, CD5 and TCRβ on DP and SP thymocytes was normal, CD44 expression was decreased on Mtorchino CD4SP and CD8SP thymocytes (Figure 8F).
evidence: Flow cytometry histograms in Figure 8F show reduced CD44 expression on Mtorchino thymocytes.

claim: CD44 expression on peripheral blood CD4+ T cells decreases in an Mtorchino allele dose-dependent manner.
source: CD44 expression on peripheral blood CD4+ T cells decreased in an Mtorchino allele dose-dependent manner (Figure 8G)
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis in Figure 8G shows gene dosage-dependent reduction in CD44 expression.

claim: CD44 expression is a highly sensitive reporter of small changes in basal mTOR activity in CD4+ T cells.
source: CD44 expression on peripheral blood CD4+ T cells decreased in an Mtorchino allele dose-dependent manner (Figure 8G), demonstrating that CD44 expression is a highly sensitive reporter of small changes in basal mTOR activity in CD4+ T cells.
evidence: The dose-dependent relationship between Mtor genotype and CD44 expression demonstrates sensitivity as a reporter.

claim: Mice with a neo-insertion in an Mtor intron that decreases Mtor mRNA approximately 70% show a similar selective lowering of CD44 on CD4+ T cells.
source: This conclusion is reinforced by supplementary data from two studies: mice with a neo-insertion in an Mtor intron that decreases Mtor mRNA approximately 70% show a similar selective lowering of CD44 on CD4+ T cells (Zhang et al., 2011)
evidence: The manuscript cites published data from another Mtor hypomorphic model showing similar CD44 reduction.

claim: CD44 levels are reduced on naïve, CD62L-positive T cells that are deficient for the mTOR activator Rheb or deficient for the mTOR-interacting protein Rictor.
source: This conclusion is reinforced by supplementary data from two studies: mice with a neo-insertion in an Mtor intron that decreases Mtor mRNA approximately 70% show a similar selective lowering of CD44 on CD4+ T cells (Zhang et al., 2011) and CD44 levels are also reduced on naïve, CD62L-positive T cells that are deficient for the mTOR activator Rheb or deficient for the mTOR-interacting protein Rictor (Delgoffe et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites published data from genetic models of mTOR pathway components showing CD44 reduction.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of mTOR with rapamycin results in a dose-dependent decrease in CD44 expression on wildtype and Rasgrp1Anaef thymocytes.
source: Furthermore, we found that pharmacological inhibition of mTOR with rapamycin in mice treated with low doses that avoid toxicity (Coenen et al., 2007; Araki et al., 2009), resulted in a dose-dependent decrease in CD44 expression on wildtype and Rasgrp1Anaef thymocytes (Figure 8H).
evidence: In vivo rapamycin treatment data in Figure 8H shows dose-dependent CD44 reduction.

claim: CD44 expression is decreased on Rasgrp1−/− knockout thymocytes.
source: CD44 was elevated on Rasgrp1Anaef DP and SP thymocytes, in diametric contrast to decreased CD44 on these cells in Rasgrp1−/− knockout mice (Figure 9A,B) (Priatel et al., 2007).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 9A,B shows reduced CD44 expression in Rasgrp1−/− thymocytes.

claim: CD44 is elevated on Rasgrp1Anaef DP and SP thymocytes.
source: CD44 was elevated on Rasgrp1Anaef DP and SP thymocytes, in diametric contrast to decreased CD44 on these cells in Rasgrp1−/− knockout mice (Figure 9A,B) (Priatel et al., 2007).
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis in Figure 9A,B demonstrates increased CD44 expression on Rasgrp1Anaef thymocytes.

claim: The increased CD44 expression on naïve Rasgrp1Anaef CD4+ cells cannot be explained by a putative defect in regulatory T cells.
source: A putative defect in regulatory T cells cannot explain the increased CD44 expression on naïve Rasgrp1Anaef CD4+ cells, because in mixed chimeras bearing many wild-type Foxp3+ CD4 cells, CD44 expression was still increased on Rasgrp1Anaef but not on co-resident wild-type CD62L+ FOXP3− CD4+ splenocytes (Figure 9C).
evidence: Mixed chimera experiments in Figure 9C show cell-autonomous CD44 elevation independent of Treg presence.

claim: The cell autonomous increase in CD44 expression is detectable on Rasgrp1Anaef SP and DP thymocytes in mixed chimeras.
source: The cell autonomous increase in CD44 expression was detectable on Rasgrp1Anaef SP and DP thymocytes (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis in Figure 9—figure supplement 1A,B shows cell-intrinsic CD44 elevation in thymocytes.

claim: Elevated CD44 expression is detectable on Rasgrp1Anaef CD4+ cells expressing a transgenic TCR.
source: The cell autonomous increase in CD44 expression was detectable on Rasgrp1Anaef SP and DP thymocytes (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A,B) and even on CD4+ cells expressing a transgenic TCR (Figure 9D).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 9D shows elevated CD44 on TCR transgenic Rasgrp1Anaef cells.

claim: Elevated CD44 expression on Rasgrp1Anaef cells is selective, with no distinguishable differences in CD69 and TCRβ expression compared to wildtype.
source: Elevated CD44 expression on Rasgrp1Anaef cells was selective: there were no distinguishable differences between wildtype and Rasgrp1Anaef cells in CD69 and TCRβ, which are markers of cumulative Ras signaling (D'Ambrosio et al., 1994; Genot and Cantrell, 2000; Starr et al., 2003)
evidence: Flow cytometry comparisons show normal CD69 and TCRβ expression despite elevated CD44.

claim: CD5 expression is normal on Rasgrp1Anaef cells.
source: Elevated CD44 expression on Rasgrp1Anaef cells was selective: there were no distinguishable differences between wildtype and Rasgrp1Anaef cells in CD69 and TCRβ, which are markers of cumulative Ras signaling (D'Ambrosio et al., 1994; Genot and Cantrell, 2000; Starr et al., 2003), nor in CD5 expression, a sensitive reporter of TCR affinity and constitutive or tonic TCR signaling (Azzam et al., 1998; Mandl et al., 2013) (Figure 9E, Figure 9—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis shows comparable CD5 expression between wildtype and Rasgrp1Anaef cells.

claim: Rapamycin treatment in vivo selectively reduces the increased CD44 expression on Rasgrp1Anaef cells but does not impact TCR or CD69 expression.
source: rapamycin treatment in vivo selectively reduced the increased CD44 expression on Rasgrp1Anaef cells (Figure 8H) but did not impact TCR or CD69 expression (data not shown).
evidence: Rapamycin treatment data shows selective effect on CD44 without affecting other markers.

claim: P-S6 levels in unstimulated TCRβlow (pre-selection) DP thymocytes are modestly increased in Rasgrp1Anaef mice.
source: Consistent with the CD44 data, P-S6 levels in unstimulated TCRβlow (pre-selection) DP thymocytes were modestly increased in Rasgrp1Anaef mice whereas they were decreased in cells from Rasgrp1−/− mice (Figure 10A).
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis in Figure 10A shows elevated basal P-S6 in Rasgrp1Anaef pre-selection DP thymocytes.

claim: P-S6 levels in unstimulated TCRβlow (pre-selection) DP thymocytes are decreased in Rasgrp1−/− mice.
source: Consistent with the CD44 data, P-S6 levels in unstimulated TCRβlow (pre-selection) DP thymocytes were modestly increased in Rasgrp1Anaef mice whereas they were decreased in cells from Rasgrp1−/− mice (Figure 10A).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 10A demonstrates reduced basal P-S6 in Rasgrp1−/− thymocytes.

claim: Substantial basal P-S6 levels are present in freshly isolated lymph node cells that decrease when cells are serum-starved in vitro.
source: We investigated tonic mTOR–S6 signals and found substantial basal P-S6 levels in freshly isolated lymph node cells that decreased when cells were serum-starved in vitro (Figure 10B).
evidence: Western blot analysis in Figure 10B shows reduction in P-S6 upon in vitro resting.

claim: CD5high naïve CD4+ T cells have significantly more P-S6 than their CD5low counterparts.
source: We first sorted CD44low naïve CD4+ T cells into the most bright and most dim expression for CD5 and determined that CD5high naïve CD4+ T cells have significantly more P-S6 than their CD5low counterparts (Figure 10C).
evidence: Western blot analysis of sorted cells in Figure 10C shows higher P-S6 in CD5high cells.

claim: Basal P-S6 is increased in Rasgrp1Anaef naïve CD4+ T cells, particularly in the CD5low subset compared to wildtype cells.
source: Next, dividing CD5low and CD5high naïve CD4+ T cells in equal 50–50% splits revealed that basal P-S6 was increased in Rasgrp1Anaef, particularly in the CD5low subset compared to wildtype cells (Figure 10D).
evidence: Western blot analysis in Figure 10D demonstrates elevated basal P-S6 in Rasgrp1Anaef cells, especially in CD5low subset.

claim: CD5 expression on wildtype CD4+ CD62L+ Foxp3− T cells decreases in MHCII-deficient hosts.
source: Maintenance of CD5 expression on T cells requires contact with self pMHC (Smith et al., 2001; Mandl et al., 2012) and, as expected, CD5 expression on wildtype CD4+ CD62L+ Foxp3− T cells decreased in MHCII-deficient hosts (Figure 10E)
evidence: Adoptive transfer experiments in Figure 10E show reduced CD5 expression in MHCII-deficient recipients.

claim: CD44 levels on adoptively transferred T cells are similar irrespective of MHCII expression in the adoptive hosts.
source: By contrast, CD44 levels were similar irrespective of MHCII expression in the adoptive hosts, and CD44 levels remained higher on Rasgrp1Anaef than co-transferred wild-type cells in both contexts (Figure 10E).
evidence: Adoptive transfer data in Figure 10E shows maintained CD44 levels regardless of host MHCII expression.

claim: CD44 levels remain higher on Rasgrp1Anaef than co-transferred wild-type cells in both MHCII-sufficient and MHCII-deficient hosts.
source: By contrast, CD44 levels were similar irrespective of MHCII expression in the adoptive hosts, and CD44 levels remained higher on Rasgrp1Anaef than co-transferred wild-type cells in both contexts (Figure 10E).
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis in Figure 10E demonstrates persistent CD44 elevation on Rasgrp1Anaef cells independent of MHCII.

claim: The Rasgrp1Anaef-driven increase in CD44 is at least partially independent of triggering of TCRs by self-pMHC.
source: The fact that the Rasgrp1Anaef–driven increase in CD44 is retained in the absence of MHCII suggests that this tonic signal is at least partially independent of triggering of TCRs by self-pMHC.
evidence: The persistence of elevated CD44 in MHCII-deficient hosts indicates TCR-independent signaling.

claim: The Mtorchino mutation abolishes the Rasgrp1Anaef-driven increase in CD44 expression in naïve CD4+ splenocytes.
source: Using a CD62L+ Foxp3− gate to resolve naïve CD4+ splenocytes, we found that the Mtorchino mutation abolished the Rasgrp1Anaef–driven increase in CD44 expression in these naïve T cells (Figure 11A).
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis in Figure 11A shows normalization of CD44 expression in Rasgrp1Anaef Mtorchino double mutants.

claim: The Mtorchino mutation alone results in a decrease in numbers of splenocytes, including CD4+ cells.
source: The Mtorchino mutation alone resulted in a decrease in numbers of splenocytes, including CD4+ cells, as was observed in mice with reduced Mtor mRNA (Zhang et al., 2011), but the relative proportions of the CD4+ subsets examined were normal (Figure 11B).
evidence: Quantification in Figure 11B shows reduced total cell numbers but normal subset proportions in Mtorchino mice.

claim: The relative proportions of CD4+ subsets are normal in Mtorchino mice.
source: The Mtorchino mutation alone resulted in a decrease in numbers of splenocytes, including CD4+ cells, as was observed in mice with reduced Mtor mRNA (Zhang et al., 2011), but the relative proportions of the CD4+ subsets examined were normal (Figure 11B).
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis in Figure 11B demonstrates normal CD4+ subset frequencies in Mtorchino mice.

claim: The accumulation of CD44hi Foxp3− CD4+ splenocytes, including the prominent PD-1+ Helios+ subset, is corrected down to normal numbers in Rasgrp1Anaef Mtorchino double mutants.
source: Whereas Rasgrp1Anaef mice with normal mTOR accumulated a high frequency of CD44hi Foxp3− CD4+ splenocytes, including the prominent PD-1+ Helios+ subset, this was corrected down to normal numbers in Rasgrp1Anaef Mtorchino double mutants (Figure 11B,C).
evidence: Flow cytometry and quantification in Figure 11B,C show normalization of CD44hi and PD-1+ Helios+ cell numbers in double mutants.

claim: In bone marrow chimeras bearing Rasgrp1Anaef Mtorchino double-mutant hematopoietic cells, the frequency of animals with antinuclear autoantibodies is corrected to the low frequency observed in control chimeras with wildtype Rasgrp1 and Mtor.
source: Moreover, in bone marrow chimeras bearing Rasgrp1Anaef Mtorchino double-mutant hematopoietic cells, the frequency of animals with antinuclear autoantibodies was corrected to the low frequency observed in control chimeras with wildtype Rasgrp1 and Mtor (Figure 11D).
evidence: ANA testing in chimeric mice in Figure 11D shows normalization of autoantibody frequency in double mutants.

claim: Accumulation of CD44hi Helios+ PD-1+ CD4+ cells and autoantibodies induced by Rasgrp1Anaef is sensitive to small differences in mTOR signaling.
source: Collectively, these results establish that accumulation of CD44hi Helios+ PD-1+ CD4+ cells and autoantibodies induced by Rasgrp1Anaef is sensitive to small differences in mTOR signaling.
evidence: The rescue of multiple phenotypes by the Mtorchino mutation demonstrates mTOR-dependence.

claim: Rasgrp1 plays a critical role in the activation of Ras.
source: Although Rasgrp1 plays a critical role in the activation of Ras, relatively little is known about its regulation in T lymphocytes or the in vivo importance of such regulation.
evidence: The statement is presented as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Rasgrp1's GEF activity is enhanced by inducible phosphorylation of threonine 184.
source: In addition to membrane recruitment via its DAG-binding C1 domain (Ebinu et al., 1998), Rasgrp1's GEF activity is enhanced by inducible phosphorylation of threonine 184 (Roose et al., 2005; Zheng et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites published studies demonstrating T184 phosphorylation enhances Rasgrp1 activity.

claim: Rasgrp1 contains a pair of EF hands, motifs that often bind calcium, which induces conformational changes.
source: Interestingly, Rasgrp1 also contains a pair of EF hands, motifs that often bind calcium, which induces conformational changes (Gifford et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on EF hand structure and function.

claim: Rasgrp1 has been reported to bind calcium in vitro.
source: Rasgrp1 has been reported to bind calcium in vitro (Ebinu et al., 1998).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published report of calcium binding by Rasgrp1.

claim: In chicken DT40 B cells, the first EF1 domain enables the recruitment function of a C-terminal PT domain that cooperates with the C1 domain to recruit Rasgrp1 to the membrane.
source: In chicken DT40 B cells, the first EF1 domain enables the recruitment function of a C-terminal PT domain (plasma membrane targeting domain) that cooperates with the C1 domain to recruit Rasgrp1 to the membrane (Tazmini et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites published work on Rasgrp1 membrane recruitment mechanisms in B cells.

claim: The PT domain contribution to Rasgrp1 membrane recruitment is substantial in BCR-stimulated B cell lines, very modest in T cell lines, and negligible in fibroblasts.
source: Notably, the PT domain contribution is substantial in BCR-stimulated B cell lines, very modest in T cell lines, and negligible in fibroblasts (Beaulieu et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites published data on cell type-specific differences in PT domain function.

claim: Genetic deletion of Rasgrp1's 200 C-terminal amino acids reduces the formation of mature thymocytes in Rasgrp1d/d mice.
source: Genetic deletion of Rasgrp1's 200 C-terminal amino acids reduces the formation of mature thymocytes in Rasgrp1d/d mice (Fuller et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites published work on the functional importance of Rasgrp1's C-terminus.

claim: Rasgrp1's C terminus contains a coiled-coil dimerization domain.
source: Our recent structural studies revealed that Rasgrp1's C terminus contains a coiled-coil dimerization domain (Iwig et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites their own recent structural studies revealing the dimerization domain.

claim: Rasgrp1 dimerization plays an important role in controlling Rasgrp1's activity.
source: Rasgrp1 dimerization plays an important role in controlling Rasgrp1's activity; the second EF hand of one Rasgrp1 molecule packs against the C1 domain of a second molecule in a manner that is incompatible with DAG-binding whereas calcium binding to the first EF hand is predicted to unlock this autoinhibitory dimer interface (Iwig et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites their structural work demonstrating the regulatory role of dimerization.

claim: The second EF hand of one Rasgrp1 molecule packs against the C1 domain of a second molecule in a manner that is incompatible with DAG-binding.
source: Rasgrp1 dimerization plays an important role in controlling Rasgrp1's activity; the second EF hand of one Rasgrp1 molecule packs against the C1 domain of a second molecule in a manner that is incompatible with DAG-binding whereas calcium binding to the first EF hand is predicted to unlock this autoinhibitory dimer interface (Iwig et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites structural data showing the autoinhibitory dimer interface.

claim: Calcium binding to the first EF hand is predicted to unlock the autoinhibitory dimer interface of Rasgrp1.
source: Rasgrp1 dimerization plays an important role in controlling Rasgrp1's activity; the second EF hand of one Rasgrp1 molecule packs against the C1 domain of a second molecule in a manner that is incompatible with DAG-binding whereas calcium binding to the first EF hand is predicted to unlock this autoinhibitory dimer interface (Iwig et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites structural modeling predicting calcium-mediated relief of autoinhibition.

claim: A link between Rasgrp1 and mTOR signaling has been proposed.
source: Lastly, it is unknown if Rasgrp1 may signal to pathways other than the canonical Rasgrp1-Ras-RAF-MEK-ERK cascade, although a link between Rasgrp1 and mTOR (mechanistic target of rapamycin) signaling has been proposed (Gorentla et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published proposal of a Rasgrp1-mTOR connection.

claim: Older Rasgrp1-deficient mice develop splenomegaly and autoantibodies.
source: Older Rasgrp1-deficient (Coughlin et al., 2005) and Rasgrp1d/d mice (Fuller et al., 2012) develop splenomegaly and autoantibodies.
evidence: The manuscript cites published reports of autoimmune phenotypes in Rasgrp1-deficient mice.

claim: Complete deletion or truncation of Rasgrp1 greatly decreases T cell development in the thymus.
source: In these mouse models, the complete deletion or truncation of Rasgrp1 greatly decreases T cell development in the thymus (Dower et al., 2000; Fuller et al., 2012)
evidence: The manuscript cites published data on thymic defects in Rasgrp1-deficient mice.

claim: Complete deletion or truncation of Rasgrp1 results in peripheral T cell lymphopenia followed by accumulation of CD44hi CD62Llo CD4+ T cells.
source: In these mouse models, the complete deletion or truncation of Rasgrp1 greatly decreases T cell development in the thymus (Dower et al., 2000; Fuller et al., 2012), resulting in peripheral T cell lymphopenia followed by accumulation of CD44hi CD62Llo CD4+ T cells (Priatel et al., 2007; Fuller et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites published observations of peripheral T cell phenotypes in Rasgrp1-deficient mice.

claim: Autoimmune phenotypes in Rasgrp1-deficient and Rasgrp1d/d mice have been attributed to compromised T cell selection in the thymus and compensatory expansion of peripheral T cells in response to lymphopenia and/or chronic infection.
source: Autoimmune phenotypes caused by these mutations have been attributed to compromised T cell selection in the thymus and compensatory expansion of peripheral T cells in response to lymphopenia and/or chronic infection.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the prevailing explanation for autoimmunity in Rasgrp1-deficient models from the literature.

claim: The SKG allele of ZAP-70 has reduced binding-affinity for phospho-TCRζ and leads to autoimmune arthritis in mice.
source: For example, an SKG allele of the kinase ZAP-70 has reduced binding-affinity for phospho-TCRζ and leads to autoimmune arthritis in mice (Sakaguchi et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript cites published work on the SKG ZAP-70 mutation and its autoimmune consequences.

claim: Point mutations in ZAP70's catalytic domain that reduce kinase activity to intermediate levels diminish thymic deletion and Foxp3+ Treg differentiation but preserve peripheral T cell activation, resulting in autoantibody formation and hyper-IgE production.
source: Point mutations in ZAP70's catalytic domain that reduce kinase activity to intermediate levels diminish thymic deletion and Foxp3+ Treg differentiation but preserve peripheral T cell activation, resulting in autoantibody formation and hyper-IgE production (Siggs et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites published work on hypomorphic ZAP70 mutations and their immunological consequences.

claim: Mutation of a single tyrosine in LAT (LATY136F) results in hyperproliferative lymphocytes of a TH2 type.
source: Mutation of a single tyrosine in LAT (LATY136F) results in hyperproliferative lymphocytes of a TH2 type (Aguado et al., 2002; Sommers et al., 2002).
evidence: The manuscript cites published work on the LAT Y136F mutation and its effects on lymphocyte function.

claim: In ZAP-70 and LAT mutant mice, peripheral T cell dysregulation is tied to, and potentially explained by, profound deficits in thymic T cell formation.
source: In each of these cases, peripheral T cell dysregulation is tied to, and potentially explained by, profound deficits in thymic T cell formation.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes a common feature of previously described signaling mutants.

claim: Most people inherit approximately 12,000 missense gene variants.
source: Single nucleotide variants that cause amino acid substitutions (missense variants; SNVs) or modify the level of gene expression rather than knocking out protein expression are a major form of human genetic variation: most people inherit ∼12,000 missense gene variants (The 1000 Genomes Project Consortium, 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites data from the 1000 Genomes Project on the prevalence of missense variants.

claim: Common tag SNVs near RASGRP1 are associated with susceptibility to autoimmune (Type 1) diabetes.
source: Common tag SNVs near RASGRP1 are associated with susceptibility to autoimmune (Type 1) diabetes and to thyroid autoantibodies in Graves' disease (Qu et al., 2009; Plagnol et al., 2011)
evidence: The manuscript cites published genetic association studies linking RASGRP1 region SNPs to autoimmune diseases.

claim: Common tag SNVs near RASGRP1 are associated with thyroid autoantibodies in Graves' disease.
source: Common tag SNVs near RASGRP1 are associated with susceptibility to autoimmune (Type 1) diabetes and to thyroid autoantibodies in Graves' disease (Qu et al., 2009; Plagnol et al., 2011)
evidence: The manuscript cites published genetic association studies linking RASGRP1 region SNPs to Graves' disease.

claim: 13 unstudied RASGRP1 missense SNVs are currently listed in public databases.
source: Common tag SNVs near RASGRP1 are associated with susceptibility to autoimmune (Type 1) diabetes and to thyroid autoantibodies in Graves' disease (Qu et al., 2009; Plagnol et al., 2011), while 13 unstudied RASGRP1 missense SNVs are currently listed in public databases.
evidence: The manuscript states the number of uncharacterized RASGRP1 missense variants in databases.

claim: Increased mTOR activity is essential for the Rasgrp1Anaef T cell dysregulation.
source: CD44 expression, CD4+ T cell subset ratios and serum autoantibodies all returned to normal in Rasgrp1AnaefMtorchino double-mutant mice, demonstrating that increased mTOR activity is essential for the Rasgrp1Anaef T cell dysregulation.
evidence: The rescue of multiple phenotypes by reducing mTOR activity demonstrates its essential role.

claim: Rasgrp1Anaef reveals an important in vivo regulatory function of Rasgrp1's EF hands.
source: Here we describe the analysis of a novel ENU-induced missense variant, Rasgrp1Anaef that reveals an important in vivo regulatory function of Rasgrp1's EF hands.
evidence: The manuscript's findings demonstrate a regulatory role for the EF hands through analysis of the Anaef mutation.

claim: Rasgrp1Anaef is distinct from previously described autoimmune mutations in Rasgrp1, Zap70 or Lat, as it has no detectable effect on thymocyte development in mice with normal TCR repertoires.
source: Rasgrp1Anaef is distinct from previously described autoimmune mutations in Rasgrp1, Zap70 or Lat, as Rasgrp1Anaef has no detectable effect on thymocyte development in mice with normal TCR repertoires, but results in peripheral accumulation of a distinct population of Helios+ PD-1+ T-helper cells and production of anti-nuclear autoantibodies.
evidence: The manuscript contrasts Rasgrp1Anaef with other signaling mutants based on normal thymic development.

claim: Rasgrp1Anaef results in peripheral accumulation of a distinct population of Helios+ PD-1+ T-helper cells.
source: Rasgrp1Anaef is distinct from previously described autoimmune mutations in Rasgrp1, Zap70 or Lat, as Rasgrp1Anaef has no detectable effect on thymocyte development in mice with normal TCR repertoires, but results in peripheral accumulation of a distinct population of Helios+ PD-1+ T-helper cells and production of anti-nuclear autoantibodies.
evidence: The manuscript describes the unique peripheral T cell phenotype in Rasgrp1Anaef mice.

claim: In contrast to Rasgrp1 deletion, the Rasgrp1Anaef missense variant increases tonic mTOR signaling in naïve CD4+ T cells.
source: In contrast to Rasgrp1 deletion, the Rasgrp1Anaef missense variant increases tonic mTOR signaling in naïve CD4+ T cells.
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates increased basal mTOR-S6 signaling in Rasgrp1Anaef naïve CD4+ cells.

claim: Genetic reduction of mTOR function in Rasgrp1Anaef mice normalizes CD44 expression on naïve CD4+ T cells.
source: Genetic reduction of mTOR function in Rasgrp1Anaef mice normalizes CD44 expression on naïve CD4+ T cells and abolishes excessive accumulation of effector T cells and autoantibodies
evidence: The double mutant analysis demonstrates mTOR-dependence of the CD44 phenotype.

claim: Genetic reduction of mTOR function in Rasgrp1Anaef mice abolishes excessive accumulation of effector T cells and autoantibodies.
source: Genetic reduction of mTOR function in Rasgrp1Anaef mice normalizes CD44 expression on naïve CD4+ T cells and abolishes excessive accumulation of effector T cells and autoantibodies
evidence: The double mutant analysis shows rescue of effector T cell accumulation and autoantibodies.

claim: Increased mTOR activity plays a central role in driving immune dysregulation in Rasgrp1Anaef mice.
source: Genetic reduction of mTOR function in Rasgrp1Anaef mice normalizes CD44 expression on naïve CD4+ T cells and abolishes excessive accumulation of effector T cells and autoantibodies, demonstrating a central role for increased mTOR activity in driving immune dysregulation in Rasgrp1Anaef mice.
evidence: The rescue of multiple phenotypes by reducing mTOR demonstrates its central role in pathogenesis.
